items.title: Discourse's Defeat Completes: Visible Collapse and the Nine Faults of Speech

items.zh: 言屈者，如立論者為對論者之所屈伏。或託餘事方便而退，或引外言，或現憤發，或現瞋恚，或現憍慢，或現所覆，或現惱害，或現不忍，或現不信，或復默然，或復憂慼，或竦肩伏面，或沈思詞窮。
items.en: Being verbally cornered: as when one positing a thesis, overcome by the opponent, resorts to some pretext and withdraws under that cover, or brings in irrelevant talk, or displays outburst, or displays hostility, or displays arrogance, or exposes the other's hidden faults, or displays malice, or displays intolerance, or displays distrust, or falls silent, or falls into visible dejection, or slumps the shoulders and lowers the face, or sinks into thought with words utterly exhausted.

items.zh: 假託餘事方便而退者，謂捨前所立，更託餘宗；捨先因、喻、同類、異類、現量、比量及正教量，更託餘因乃至正教。引外言者，謂捨所論事，論說飲食、王臣、盜賊、衢路、倡穢等事，假託外緣，捨本所立，以遣他難。現憤發者，謂以麁獷不遜等言，擯對論者。現瞋恚者，謂以怨報之言，責對論者。現憍慢者，謂以卑賤種族等言，毀對論者。現所覆者，謂以發他所覆惡行之言，舉對論者。現惱害者，謂以害酷怨言，罵對論者。現不忍者，謂發怨言，怖對論者。現不信者，謂以毀壞行言，謗對論者。或默然者，謂語業頓盡。或憂慼者，謂意業焦惱。竦肩伏面者：謂身業威嚴而頓萎顇。沈思詞窮者，謂才辯俱竭。
items.en: 'Withdrawing on the pretext of some other matter' means abandoning what one first established and turning to another position; abandoning one's earlier reason, example, similar case, dissimilar case, direct perception, inference, and authoritative teaching, and turning to some other reason and so on through authoritative teaching. 'Bringing in outside talk' means abandoning the matter under discussion and talking about food and drink, kings and ministers, thieves, roads, entertainers, and the like, using outside matters as a pretext to abandon what one first established and to evade the other's challenge. 'Showing irritation' means rebuffing the opponent with coarse and insolent words. 'Showing anger' means reproaching the opponent with words of retaliation. 'Showing arrogance' means disparaging the opponent with words about his low birth and so on. 'Showing what is hidden' means attacking the opponent with words that expose his hidden misdeeds. 'Showing malice' means abusing the opponent with cruel and spiteful words. 'Showing intolerance' means frightening the opponent with words of enmity. 'Showing distrust' means slandering the opponent with words that disparage his conduct. 'Falling silent' means that one's verbal activity suddenly ends. 'Being dejected' means that one's mental activity is scorched and troubled. 'Slumping the shoulders and lowering the face' means that the dignity of one's bodily activity suddenly withers. 'Sinking into thought with words exhausted' means that both wit and eloquence are spent.

items.zh: 由如是等十三種事，當知言屈。前二，妄行矯亂；中七，發起邪行；後四，計行窮盡。是名言屈，墮在負處。
items.en: By these thirteen signs, know this is being verbally cornered. The first two are a false attempt to confuse the exchange; the middle seven are the arising of misconduct; the last four are the exhaustion of one's stratagems. This is called being verbally cornered, and it falls into defeat.

items.zh: 言過者，謂立論者為九種過污染其言，故名言過。何等為九？一、雜亂，二、麁獷，三、不辯了，四、無限量，五、非義相應，六、不以時，七、不決定，八、不顯了，九、不相續。
items.en: Speech itself carrying a fault: it means the one positing the thesis has their speech tainted by nine kinds of fault, and so it is called a fault of speech. What are the nine? First, disorder; second, coarseness; third, failing to make oneself understood; fourth, lacking proper measure; fifth, incoherence with the meaning; sixth, being out of sequence; seventh, indecisiveness; eighth, lack of clarity; and ninth, discontinuity.

items.zh: 雜亂者，謂捨所論事，雜說異語。麁獷者，謂憤發掉舉及躁急掉舉。不辯了者，謂若法若義，眾及對論所不領悟。無限量者，謂所說義言詞復重，或復減少。非義相應者，當知有十種。一、無義，二、違義，三、損理，四、與所成等，五、招集過難，六、不得義利，七、義無次序，八、義不決定，九、成立能成，十、順不稱理諸邪惡論。非時者，謂所應說，前後不次。不決定者，謂立已復毀，毀而復立，速疾轉換，難可了知。不顯了者，謂言招譏弄，不領而答；先為典語後為俗語，或先俗語後復典語。不相續者，謂於中間言詞斷絕。凡所言論犯此九失，是名言過，墮在負處。
items.en: Disorder: abandoning the matter under discussion and mixing in unrelated talk. Failing to make oneself understood: neither the statement nor its meaning is grasped by the assembly or by the opponent. Indecisiveness: positing a point, then retracting it, then positing it again, switching back and forth so rapidly it becomes impossible to follow. Whatever discourse falls into these nine faults is called a fault of speech, and it falls into defeat.

items.title: Discourse's Release Opens: Weighing Gain and Loss Before Speaking

items.zh: 論出離者，謂立論者，先應以彼三種觀察觀察論端，方興言論，或不興論，名論出離。三種觀察者，一、觀察得失，二、觀察時眾，三、觀察善巧及不善巧。
items.en: Discourse's release: it means that one positing a thesis should first apply three kinds of examination at the outset of discourse, and only then either take up discourse or refrain from it — this is called discourse's release [from faults]. The three examinations: first, examining gain and loss; second, examining the assembly at hand; and third, examining one's own skill or lack of it.

items.zh: 觀察得失者，謂立論者方興論端，先當觀察我立是論，將無自損、損他及俱損耶？不生現法後法及俱罪耶？勿起身心諸憂苦耶？莫由此故，執持刀杖、鬪罵諍訟、諂誑妄語而發起耶？將無種種惡不善法而生長耶？非不利益安樂若自若他及多眾耶？非不憐愍諸世間耶？不因此故，諸天世人無義無利不安樂耶？
items.en: Examining gain and loss: it means that, before beginning discourse, one should first ask: will this discourse harm myself, or harm the other, or harm us both? Will it produce fault in this life, in future lives, or in both? Will it stir up affliction of body or mind? Will it, through this very act, lead to violence, quarreling, deceit, and false speech? Will it cause various unwholesome states to grow? Will it fail to bring benefit and ease to myself, to the other, and to the many? Will it fail to come from compassion for the world? And will it, because of this, leave gods and humans without benefit, without gain, and without ease?

items.zh: 彼立論者如是觀時，若自了知我所立論，能為自損，乃至天人無義無利，亦無安樂；便自思勉，不應立論。若如是知我所立論，不為自損，乃至能引天人義利及與安樂；便自思勉，當立正論。是名第一或作不作論出離相。
items.en: When one positing a thesis examines in this way, if one recognises that this discourse would harm oneself and, further, bring no benefit, no gain, and no ease to gods and humans, one should exert oneself in reflection and not take up the discourse. But if one recognises that this discourse would not harm oneself and, further, would bring benefit, gain, and ease to gods and humans, one should exert oneself in reflection and take up right discourse. This is called the first mark of discourse's release, concerning whether or not to act.

blocks.text: Today completes the ways a debater loses and opens the sixth heading, **release from debate** (論出離). The key idea of the second is unexpected: sometimes the right outcome of examining a debate is not to have it.

A debater who is "cornered" shows it in many ways: changing the subject, losing composure, falling silent, and others. One is exposing the opponent's hidden faults. Master Cháng Bǎi: unable to win, one brings up the other's past mistakes to humiliate him. Another is "uttering words of enmity to frighten the opponent". Venerable Miào Jìng: threatening him. (Ru-Yi's "refusal to accept defeat" softens it.)
Every one of these is familiar from ordinary arguments. The treatise treats them as signs that the argument is already lost, whatever the volume.

Speech has nine faults, among them confusion, impetuosity, and speaking "out of order". Venerable Miào Jìng: an argument "with no order from front to back, a sentence here, a sentence there". Good argument has structure.

The sixth heading is 論出離. Ru-Yi translates "withdrawal", which suggests simply leaving. Both teachers read it as **release from faults**. Venerable Miào Jìng: "coming out of fault, not committing it". Whether one argues or refrains, either can be release.

Before debating, one weighs gain and loss: will this debate benefit myself or others, or only cause harm? If harm, one refrains. Venerable Miào Jìng on "exerting oneself in reflection": "I won't do this; my mind wants to, but I won't." Restraint here is a choice made after examination, not timidity.

Most arguments we have are not formal debates. But the test applies: before contesting a point, ask whether it will help anyone. If not, the treatise's advice is to let it go. This is the same skill as letting a distracting thought go in meditation (Day 98): seeing that pursuing it brings no benefit.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain "exposing the other's hidden faults" among the signs of being cornered?
options: unable to out-argue the opponent, one exposes his past wrongs to humiliate him
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: unable to win, one brings up the other's past mistakes so that he can't save face. Venerable Miào Jìng: "A nasty move — exposing what was hidden." f15 omits the itemised glosses.

quiz.q: The English renders 現不忍 as "refusal to accept defeat." What do the treatise and Venerable Miào Jìng say?
options: the treatise: "uttering words of enmity to frighten the opponent" — threatening him
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Uttering hateful words to frighten the other — frightening and threatening him." The omitted text defines it thus. Likewise "displays disbelief" is really slandering the opponent's conduct.

quiz.q: The English renders 不以時 as "wrong timing." What is the treatise's own definition, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: "what should be said is out of order" — the argument has no sequence, a sentence here, a sentence there
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the argument one should present has no order from front to back — confused, a sentence here and a sentence there. The omitted definition concerns sequence, not timing.

quiz.q: The English calls 論出離 "Discourse's withdrawal," suggesting pulling out. How do the two teachers explain 出離?
options: release from faults — after examination one avoids error; whether one argues or refrains, both are 出離
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "It is release from faults — coming out of fault, not committing it; that is how one should act." Master Cháng Bǎi agrees. The treatise: taking up discourse, or refraining, is called 論出離.

quiz.q: After examining gain and loss, one "exerts oneself in reflection" and refrains. How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain 思勉?
options: reflecting and restraining oneself — wanting to do it, yet choosing not to
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "One reflects and pushes oneself — I won't do this; my mind wants to, but I won't." Master Cháng Bǎi: the seventh question checks motive — compassion for the world, or a desire to win.
